items.prompt: A team replaces their single overloaded server with a bigger, more powerful machine. What kind of scaling is this?
items.explanation: Making one machine bigger (more CPU/RAM) is vertical scaling; the number of servers stays the same.
items.reference:
Two ways to grow
🖥️ Vertical — one machine, bigger (hard ceiling, single point of failure)
➕ Horizontal — more machines, traffic split (roughly linear, survives one loss)

Why: vertical scaling hits a ceiling and keeps one failure domain; horizontal scaling spreads both load and failure.
items.reflection: A restaurant can buy a bigger stove or open a second kitchen. Where else have you seen a choice between making one thing bigger and running several copies of it, and what did each choice cost?

items.prompt: What does a stateless server hold in its own memory?
choices: A full copy of the database
Nothing another server would need to handle that user's next request
Only the code of other servers
items.explanation: Anything request-specific that must persist lives in a shared place.
items.reference:
Stateful vs stateless
🔒 Stateful — session lives only in one server's memory
🔓 Stateless — session lives in a store every server reaches

Why: any server must be able to serve a user's next request, so what the next request needs cannot live only in one server's memory.
items.reflection: A waiter who memorizes your order is useless if a different waiter brings the food; a written ticket works for anyone. Where in daily life does 'who remembers it' decide whether you can swap people out?

items.prompt: What rule does round robin follow?
choices: Cycle through servers in a fixed order
Pick a random server each time and remember it
items.explanation: A, B, C, A, B, C, ...
items.reference:
Algorithms at a glance
🔁 Round robin — fixed rotation, no state beyond a cursor
📉 Least connections — fewest in-flight requests wins
⚖️ Weighted — bigger server, bigger share

Why: the algorithm should match how uneven your servers and requests really are.
items.reflection: Checkout lines at a supermarket: one rule is 'next free till in order', another is 'shortest queue'. Where else do you choose between a fixed rotation and looking at the current load, and what does each assume?
